units.t: The Spotlight Effect.
Part one. The shirt experiment.
Picture this. You walk into a room full of people, and you're wearing a T-shirt with a large, slightly embarrassing face printed on the front.
Your cheeks go warm.
You're certain every single person has noticed.
Now here's the question this lesson is built around.
How many of them actually did?
In the late 1990s, the psychologist Thomas Gilovich and his colleagues at Cornell University decided to find out.
They asked university students to put on a T-shirt showing the singer Barry Manilow.
At the time, for a college student, this was about the least cool shirt imaginable.
Each student then walked into a room where other students were already sitting and filling in questionnaires.
They stayed a short while, then were led back out.
Afterwards the researchers asked the shirt-wearers a simple question.
How many of the people in that room do you think noticed who was on your shirt?
The wearers guessed around half.
Then the researchers asked the people in the room.
The real figure was closer to a quarter.
The wearers had roughly doubled the attention they were getting.
Gilovich and his co-authors, Victoria Medvec and Kenneth Savitsky, gave this a name.
They called it the spotlight effect.
It's the tendency to overestimate how much other people notice our appearance and our behaviour.
We feel as though a spotlight follows us around.
In reality, the light is much dimmer, and it's pointed at lots of other people too.
Why does this happen?
The main reason is surprisingly simple.
You are the centre of your own experience.
You've been living inside your own head all day.
You know exactly what you're wearing, what you said in that meeting, and the spot on your chin you noticed in the mirror this morning.
All of that information is loud and vivid to you.
So when you imagine how others see you, you start from your own view, and then you adjust.
The trouble is, we don't adjust nearly enough.
Psychologists call this anchoring and adjustment.
Your own perspective is the anchor, and it drags your estimate towards itself.
There's a second reason too.
Everyone else in that room is also living at the centre of their own experience.
They're thinking about their questionnaire, their own shirt, their own plans for lunch.
Their attention is already full.
You're a small part of their day, not the headline.
So that's the first idea to take away.
The attention you feel is not the attention you get.
In the next part, we'll look at a close cousin of the spotlight effect.
It shows up whenever you're nervous, and it may change how you feel about public speaking.
Part two. The illusion of transparency.
Think about the last time you had to speak in front of a group.
Maybe a presentation at work, a toast at a wedding, or even asking a question at a meeting.
Your heart was racing.
Your hands felt shaky.
And you were probably convinced that everyone could see how nervous you were.
The same research team studied this feeling too.
They called it the illusion of transparency.
It's the belief that our inner states, our nerves, our thoughts and our emotions, are much more visible to other people than they actually are.
We feel transparent, like a glass jar.
We're not.
In one set of studies, Gilovich, Savitsky and Medvec had people tell lies while others watched and tried to spot the liars.
The people telling the lies consistently overestimated how many observers would catch them.
Their guilt felt obvious from the inside.
From the outside, it mostly wasn't.
Then came the part that's genuinely useful.
Kenneth Savitsky and Thomas Gilovich ran a study with people giving short public talks.
Some speakers were simply told to relax.
Others were told about the illusion of transparency.
They heard, in effect, that nerves feel obvious to the speaker but are usually hard for an audience to see.
Those informed speakers ended up feeling less anxious.
And here's the interesting bit.
Observers rated their talks as better too.
Why would knowing about the illusion help?
Because a lot of performance anxiety feeds on itself.
You feel nervous.
You believe the audience can see it.
That belief makes you more nervous, which you assume they can see even more clearly.
It's a loop.
Knowing that your nerves are mostly invisible cuts the loop.
It takes away the fear of being seen as afraid.
Here's a practical way to use this.
Next time you're nervous before speaking, try telling yourself something like this.
They can't see what I'm feeling.
Most of this is happening on the inside.
You're not pretending the nerves aren't there.
You're just correcting the story about who can see them.
One caution. The illusion of transparency doesn't mean nobody ever notices anything.
A shaky voice or a flushed face can sometimes be seen.
The point is that we tend to exaggerate it.
The audience sees a person giving a talk.
You feel a person barely holding it together.
The gap between those two pictures is usually large.
In the final part, we'll flip the whole idea around.
If people notice our flaws less than we think, what about the good impressions we make?
It turns out we get those wrong as well, and not in the direction you might expect.
Part three. The liking gap.
Imagine you've just met someone new.
Maybe it's a neighbour, or a colleague from another team.
You chat for a few minutes.
Afterwards, walking away, you replay the conversation.
Did I talk too much?
Was that joke weird?
Did they actually like me?
In 2018, a group of researchers led by Erica Boothby, working with colleagues including Gus Cooney and Gillian Sandstrom, studied exactly this moment.
They paired up strangers and had them talk.
Then they asked each person two things.
How much did you like your partner?
And how much do you think your partner liked you?
The pattern was striking.
People consistently underestimated how much their conversation partner liked them.
The researchers called this the liking gap.
And it wasn't a one-off.
It showed up in short chats in the lab, and it showed up in longer conversations.
In one study, they followed university students who had just started living together, and the gap lasted for months.
Why would this happen?
Part of it is the same spotlight at work.
After a conversation, we focus on our own awkward moments.
The pause that felt too long.
The thing we wish we'd said differently.
Our partner, meanwhile, was busy worrying about their own awkward moments.
They barely registered ours.
So we judge ourselves on our worst bits, while they judge us on the overall feel of the chat, which was usually warm.
Put all three ideas together and a clear picture forms.
We think people notice our embarrassing moments more than they do.
That's the spotlight effect.
We think people can see our nerves more than they can.
That's the illusion of transparency.
And we think people like us less than they actually do.
That's the liking gap.
In each case, the harshest critic is the one inside our own head.
So what do you do with this?
Here are three small experiments for the week ahead.
First, the next time you feel self-conscious about something you're wearing or something you said, ask yourself, how much would I have noticed if someone else did this?
Usually the honest answer is, barely at all.
Second, before your next presentation or tricky conversation, remind yourself that your nerves are mostly invisible.
Third, after you meet someone new, assume they liked you a bit more than you think.
The research suggests you'll usually be right.
Let's recap. The spotlight effect: we overestimate how much others notice us.
The illusion of transparency: we overestimate how visible our feelings are.
The liking gap: we underestimate how much people enjoy our company.
The spotlight is dimmer than it feels, and that's genuinely good news.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. In the Cornell T-shirt study, wearers guessed about half the room noticed their shirt. Roughly how many actually did?
Answer. About a quarter. The wearers roughly doubled the attention they were getting.
Question two. What's the name for the belief that other people can see our nerves and emotions more clearly than they really can?
Answer. The illusion of transparency.
Question three. After meeting someone new, do people tend to overestimate or underestimate how much the other person liked them?
Answer. Underestimate. That's the liking gap.
That's the end of The Spotlight Effect. Nicely done.
